## Ezekiel 16:1–21 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

### Overview of the Chapter

The chapter is a long allegory (the longest in Ezekiel) in which Jerusalem/Israel is portrayed as a foundling girl rescued by God, raised, married, and lavishly adorned — only to become an unfaithful wife-prostitute. The ancient rabbis forbade public reading of this chapter because of its graphic content. Spurgeon called it "a very extraordinary chapter … a minister could scarcely read it in public." (Enduring Word; Spurgeon cited at enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

Matthew Henry summarises the chapter's design: God is justifying Himself in the desolations He is about to bring upon Jerusalem — showing the people that He punishes them only as their sins deserve. The chapter has six parts: (I) despicable beginnings (vv. 3–5); (II) God's honours and favours (vv. 6–14); (III) treacherous idolatry depicted as whoredom (vv. 15–34); (IV) threatened judgments (vv. 35–43); (V) aggravation by comparison with Sodom and Samaria (vv. 44–59); (VI) a promise of mercy to a penitent remnant (vv. 60–63). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/ezekiel-16.html)

The three main parts according to Ellicott are: the sin (vv. 3–34), the punishment (vv. 35–52), and the final restoration of Israel (vv. 53–63). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 1 — "Again the word of the LORD came to me, saying…"

- **Gill (Baptist):** The word of prophecy from the Lord came to Ezekiel under a spirit of prophecy. The "Targum" renders it similarly — a prophetic word. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 2 — "Son of man, confront Jerusalem with her abominations"

- **Gill:** "Jerusalem" here means the inhabitants of Jerusalem, representing the whole people. Their sins were "abominations" because they were abominable to God and rendered the people so. The prophet was to show them the evil nature of their sins so they might be convicted and repent. Ezekiel, though in Chaldea with the exiles, might have done this by writing to Jerusalem. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Feinberg:** "Ezekiel was charged by God to declare his message to Jerusalem as representative of all Judah, and even the entire nation." Throughout the chapter, Jerusalem is an accurate representative of the people of Israel as a whole. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Precept Austin:** The Hebrew verb translated "make known" is a Hiphil imperative — a forceful command. The Septuagint translates it with *diamarturomai*, meaning to give a solemn witness/warning. Ezekiel must make a solemn declaration. The Amplified Bible renders it "cause Jerusalem to know, understand, and realize her [idolatrous] abominations [that they] are disgusting, detestable, and shamefully vile." (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_161-14)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** Jerusalem's sins were greater than those of other nations because of her greater knowledge of God, her covenant with Him, and her trusteeship to keep His laws as receiver of the "oracles of God" (Ex 19:5–8; Rom 3:1–2). God called the prophet to put Israel's past, present, and future in perspective so that God might be recognised as just and Israel without excuse when judgment fell. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 3 — "Your origin and your birth were in the land of the Canaanites. Your father was an Amorite and your mother a Hittite."

- **Enduring Word / Taylor:** "The statement is heavy with sarcasm, however, for the term 'Canaanite' was a byword for moral decadence." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Feinberg:** "Amorite and Hittite were general names for the people of Canaan who occupied the land before Abraham…. Being the most powerful of the nations in Canaan, they represented them all." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Poole (via Enduring Word):** "Sometimes the ill nature of a father is corrected in the child by the sweetness of the mother, but you Jews were not so happy, your mother was as bad every whit as your father." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Gill:** The Jewish ancestors dwelt and sojourned in Canaan (Abraham, Isaac, Jacob). Though Abraham was a Chaldean, he was called into Canaan where Isaac and Jacob were born. Additionally, the Israelites succeeded the Canaanites in their land and imitated their manners — particularly their idolatries. The Amorite and Hittite are singled out as the worst and most wicked of the seven nations (Gen 15:16). Gill also notes that Judah married a Canaanite woman (Tamar), and the royal line descended from that union. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Wiersbe (via Precept Austin):** Many Jews were excessively proud of their heritage and called Gentiles "dogs," but the Lord reminded them that Jerusalem was once inhabited by Jebusites (Josh 15:63) and wasn't Jewish until David captured it (2 Sam 5:6–10). Even Abraham was an idol-worshipping pagan when God graciously called him (Josh 24:2–3). (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_161-14)

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Israel had a pagan origin and did not worship the one true Creator when God called them. Abraham had to be rescued from his idolatry by the Lord Himself (Josh 24:1–3). (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god)

- **Precept Austin / Ryrie:** This refers to Jerusalem's *moral genealogy* — the Amorite (Canaanite) and Hittite (a non-Semitic pagan people) represented the spiritual ancestry of her idolatrous practices, not literal blood descent. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_161-14)

---

### v. 4 — "On the day of your birth your cord was not cut, nor were you washed with water for cleansing. You were not rubbed with salt or wrapped in cloths."

- **Gill:** Alludes to what a midwife does for a newborn — cutting the navel string, washing, rubbing with salt to harden the flesh and prevent putrefaction, and swaddling to bring the limbs into shape. These things being necessary, the rabbis permitted them even on the Sabbath. This pictures the desperate, uncared-for condition of Israel in Egypt. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Feinberg:** "In salting the child the skin is rubbed with salt to make it firm and clean." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "Cutting the cord, washing, rubbing down with salt, and clothing the newborn were also customary legal acts of legitimation. In the neglect and abandonment of the infant in the open field, the parent legally relinquished all rights to and responsibilities for the child." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** The Lord found Israel having not even enjoyed the basic care needed to live past birth — washing, cutting the umbilical cord, being rubbed with salt, clothing. Ezekiel draws from mankind's common experience as well as the hygienic practices of ancient Near Eastern culture (salt rubbing). (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** The imagery conveys that no one provided Jerusalem with even the most basic care at birth. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 5 — "No one cared enough for you … you were thrown out into the open field, because you were despised on the day of your birth."

- **Gill:** Describes the helpless, forlorn, unpitied state of the Israelites in Egypt — when Pharaoh and his taskmasters showed no mercy (Ex 1:14). The "open field" may designate Egypt, where Jacob and his posterity were driven by famine. After Joseph died, they were exposed to hardships; Pharaoh's decree to kill male children led to the exposing of many infants (as with Moses). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Clarke (Methodist, via Enduring Word):** "This is an allusion to the custom of some heathen and barbarous nations, who exposed those children in the open fields to be devoured by wild beasts who had any kind of deformity, or whom they could not support." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Spurgeon (Baptist, via Enduring Word):** "Cast out into the open field, left in a wilderness where it is not likely that any should pass by, thrown where the cold can smite by night and the heat can blast by day, left where the wild beast goeth about, seeking whom he may devour — such is the estate of human nature: unclothed, unarmed, helpless, exposed to all manner of ravenous destroyers." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** The image is of a baby girl left to die of exposure — a practice all too common in the pagan culture of Babylon in Ezekiel's day. The people were originally helpless and hopeless. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god)

- **Gill (applicatory):** All this may be applied to the state and condition of men by nature — even God's elect, whose extraction is from fallen man, conceived in sin, unable to be washed or clothed by their parents, in a hopeless and helpless condition, loathsome and abominable to God and to themselves when they see their state. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 6 — "Then I passed by and saw you wallowing in your blood, and as you lay there in your blood I said to you, 'Live!' There I said to you, 'Live!'"

- **Gill:** The word translated "polluted" (KJV) or "wallowing" literally means "trodden underfoot" — denoting both pollution and distress. The Israelites were trodden underfoot by the Egyptians. When they sighed and cried because of bondage, the Lord looked on them with pity and delivered them (Ex 1:14). God preserved them and saved them alive when they were near to ruin — purely of His sovereign good will, not for any merit in them. The word for "blood" is in the plural ("bloods"), denoting abundance and great pollution. The repetition of "Live!" emphasises the urgency and passion. Gill applies this to the elect: when they are quickened by God, they are by their first birth unclean, wallowing in sin, hopeless — and God passes by (not by chance but on purpose), sees them with pity and compassion, and speaks life into them. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "He pronounces the sentence of life upon the child, otherwise sentenced to certain death. His passion is reflected in the emphatic twofold declaration, 'In your blood, live!'" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word:** God took note of Israel in their humble, hated state. It wasn't because Israel was amazing or holy — they were weak, poor, struggling, near death. But God passed by and took notice. Deuteronomy 7:7–8 explains: God did not set His love on them because they were great, but because He loved them and would keep His oath to the fathers. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Ancient Near Eastern parents adopted an infant in emergency situations by placing their hands on a newborn covered in birth fluids and declaring, "Live!" God adopted Israel when He found her exposed and in danger. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god)

---

### v. 7 — "I made you thrive like a plant of the field. You grew up and matured and became very beautiful. Your breasts were formed and your hair grew, but you were naked and bare."

- **Gill:** "I have caused thee to multiply as the bud of the field" — literally, "made thee millions," like the spires of grass in the field. This refers to Israel's multiplication in Egypt: from seventy-five persons to over six hundred thousand (Gen 46:27). "You are come to excellent ornaments" may allude to the jewels Israel brought from Egypt, or to the laws and ordinances given at Sinai, which were an "ornament of grace" (Prov 1:9). "Your breasts are fashioned and your hair is grown" expresses puberty and marriageability. "Naked and bare" — Jarchi and Kimchi interpret this of the Israelites being without the commandments. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** The reference to hair growth is to the young woman's pubic hair: "With the passing of the age of innocence and the arrival of sexual maturity, nakedness assumes moral overtones. Whereas the earlier nakedness had made the foundling vulnerable to the elements and marauding animals, now she stands exposed to dangers of a different sort." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Feinberg:** "The foundling became a beautiful young woman, yet it is stated that she was naked and bare. The implication may be that she was without wealth and without the benefits of culture and civilization, as the world sees them." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** The Lord enabled Jerusalem to thrive; her inhabitants became numerous. She eventually developed into a fine city even though she had gotten a bad start in life. During the reigns of David and Solomon, Jerusalem was one of the most highly respected cities in the ancient Near East. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 8 — "Then I passed by and saw you, and you were indeed old enough for love. So I spread My cloak over you and covered your nakedness. I pledged Myself to you, entered into a covenant with you, and you became Mine, declares the Lord GOD."

- **Gill:** "Thy time was the time of love" (KJV) — the original says "time of loves" (plural), denoting the large abundance of love shown. The Targum explains this as the time of redemption from Egypt. "I spread my skirt over thee" expresses both espousal and protection (Ruth 3:9). God entered into covenant with Israel at Horeb (Deut 29:1) — a kind of marriage contract. "Thou becamest mine" — Israel became the Lord's peculiar people (Ex 19:5). Gill applies this spiritually: the covenant of grace was made from everlasting with Christ and the elect, but is made manifest at conversion when God leads them to Christ the Mediator and shows them their interest in the blessings and promises. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Wright:** "The phrase in Ezekiel 16:8 describes the symbolic act whereby the husband took his wife under his protection (Ruth 3:9)." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Morgan:** "In earthly inter-relationships, the marriage relationship is the highest in sanctity, because it is the highest in the experience of Love. By this figure, then, God sets forth for us what His heart feels for us, and what He desires from us in return. His love is of the strongest and tenderest, and He looks for a return of that love in uttermost loyalty." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Garner-Howes Baptist Commentary:** God spread His skirt of protection over Israel to cover her nakedness and shield her from harm until He should betroth her by covenant — similar to Ruth 3:9. This refers to the betrothal union at Sinai (Ex 20:5–6; 19:2, 5; Deut 5:2). He was to love, protect, and provide; she was to love, worship, and obey, putting away all false gods. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Constable:** When Jerusalem was mature enough, the Lord made a commitment to take care of her forever (cf. Ps 132:13–17). Spreading a skirt over someone was a customary way of committing to marry in that culture. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Ligonier (Reformed):** Switching from the metaphor of God as adoptive father to God as loving husband, the Lord took her as His wife when the girl reached maturity. Centuries after Abraham and his descendants were called out of paganism, when the people had matured into a nation, the Lord married His people (Ex 12:33–42; Jer 2:2). (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god)

---

### v. 9 — "Then I bathed you with water, rinsed off your blood, and anointed you with oil."

- **Gill:** This describes God bringing Israel out of the mean, abject, servile state among the Egyptian mortar and bricks into liberty. "I thoroughly washed away thy blood" — the word signifies washing with an inundation overflowing. Spiritually, this points beyond ceremonial washings or water baptism to the thorough washing by the blood of Christ — the fountain opened for sin and uncleanness (Zech 13:1). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word:** God cleaned Israel and anointed them with fragrant oil. This is part of His care and adornment of His bride. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Constable:** The Lord prepared Jerusalem for a special relationship with Himself — He cleansed and anointed her. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### vv. 10–12 — "I clothed you in embroidered cloth … fine linen … silk … jewelry … bracelets … chain … ring in your nose, earrings … a beautiful crown upon your head."

- **Gill:** These rich adornments represent the large provision of good things God made for Israel, especially in the land of Canaan — the riches He bestowed and the flourishing kingdom He raised them to. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "Embroidered cloth…badger skin…fine linen: These expressions occur elsewhere most frequently in the descriptions of the tabernacle, its curtains, and the priestly vestments. References to the luxury leather of which her sandals are made (*tahas*) occur only in contexts involving the tabernacle." Jerusalem, the bride of Yahweh, is clothed with the garments that "clothe" the sanctuary. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Taylor:** "The badgers' skin (AV) is the same as the material used in the covering of the tabernacle (Num 4:6ff.). The various translations give sealskin (RV), porpoise skin (RV mg.), leather (RSV). 'Badger' is certainly not right, because the skin had to be both suitable for shoes and also large enough for one of them to cover the ark. The likeliest candidate is the dugong, a seal-like animal of the order Siremia, which is found in the Red Sea; its skin is used by the bedouin for making sandals." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Constable:** The Lord gave Jerusalem jewelry to make her even more beautiful — bracelets, a necklace, a ring, earrings, and a crown (cf. Gen 24:53; Ps 45:13–15; Isa 61:10). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### vv. 13–14 — "So you were adorned with gold and silver … You ate fine flour, honey, and oil. You became very beautiful and rose to be queen. Your fame spread among the nations … for it was perfect in the splendor I bestowed on you, declares the Lord GOD."

- **Enduring Word / Block:** The special food — "fine flour" and "oil" — figured prominently in the sacred offerings. Jerusalem, the bride of Yahweh, is fed with the "food" of the sanctuary's offerings. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Wiersbe:** "During the reign of King David and during Solomon's early years, Jerusalem was indeed a queenly city and Israel a prosperous kingdom. As long as Israel, Jehovah's wife, obeyed His Word and kept His covenant, He blessed her abundantly just as He promised. He gave her healthy children, fruitful flocks and herds, abundant harvests, and protection from disease, disaster, and invasion." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "Incredibly, the charge that Ezekiel would later level at the king of Tyre applied to this poor foundling: 'Your heart was lifted up on account of your beauty; you corrupted your wisdom on account of your splendor.'" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / F. B. Meyer:** "Let us dare to believe that it is so. Accept and value your position. In Christ, we are more than tolerated; we are loved. We are more than forgiven; we are arrayed in fair garments. The King greatly delights in us. In His eyes, and because His beauty is upon us, we are all fair." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Gill:** The flourishing and prosperous kingdom God raised Israel to made them famous among all nations round about. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 15 — "But because of your fame, you trusted in your beauty and played the harlot. You lavished your favors on everyone who passed by, and your beauty was theirs for the asking."

- **Enduring Word:** Pride was the root of Israel's decline. They forgot they were nothing when God found them and that He had bestowed their beauty. They trusted in the blessing rather than in God Himself. Paul captures the same principle in 1 Cor 4:7: "What do you have that you did not receive?" (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Feinberg:** Ezekiel 16:15–35 is "one of the strongest denunciations of Israel's sin found in the entire Bible. Rebukes of Israel's sin by the prophets of Israel are many and well known, but none is so vivid, vehement, sordid and piercing as these words." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Spurgeon (via Enduring Word):** "It is an ill sign in any of us when God's blessings are themselves made into idols. If thou beginnest to worship thy wealth, thy health, thy children, thy learning, or anything that God has given thee, this is exceedingly provoking to the Most High; it is a breach of the marriage covenant between thy soul and God." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "The verb [harlot, root *znh*] and other derivatives occur twenty-one times in this description of Jerusalem's unrestrained nymphomaniacal adventures with her lovers." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "Although the root *naap* [adultery] is more fitting to describe Israel's covenantal infidelity, *znh* [harlotry] offers a more forceful rhetorical tool. The innocent young woman, graciously elevated to the status of queen, has become a whore." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Taylor:** "The Christian reader may, not surprisingly, feel nauseated at the indelicate realism of Ezekiel's language, but Ezekiel meant it that way. He was telling of ugly sins and he made the parable fit the facts." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Precept Austin / Wiersbe:** When Israel became prosperous and famous, she forgot the Lord and began to use God's generous gifts for worshipping idols (Hos 2:8, 13–14; Deut 6:10–12; 8:10–20). Like the ignorant heathen nations around her, she worshipped the creation rather than the Creator (Rom 1:21–25) and abandoned her "husband" for false gods. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Constable (Evangelical):** Jerusalem became self-centred and unfaithful to the Lord; she forgot Him when she became preoccupied with His blessings (cf. Deut 6:10–12; Deut 8). Under Solomon, Jerusalem became the greatest city of her day, but Solomon led the Jerusalemites into spiritual adultery by making alliances (covenants) with other nations and establishing idolatry in the land (1 Ki 11:1–13). (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 16 — "You took some of your garments and made colorful high places for yourself, and on them you prostituted yourself. Such things should not have happened; never should they have occurred!"

- **Enduring Word:** Israel took the very blessings God adorned her with and used them to adorn places of pagan idolatry. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word / Taylor:** "The gaily decked shrines (RSV) indicate the colourful hangings of the tents that were set up at the high places (see note on Ezekiel 6:3), which were seen by Ezekiel to be places for feasting, fornication, idolatry and child-sacrifice." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Precept Austin:** "High places" (*bamah*) were associated with at least six activities — burning incense (Jer 48:35), sacrificing (2 Ki 16:4), eating sacrificial meals, praying, prostitution, and child sacrifice (Jer 7:31; 19:5; 32:35). The high places consisted of an altar, a wooden pole (Asherah), a stone pillar (*maṣṣēbâ*) for Baal, and a smaller incense altar with a tent for ritual prostitution and storage of cultic vessels. The sad refrain repeated in 2 Kings is "only the high places were not taken away" — these sites of spiritual harlotry continued to ensnare Israel. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Precept Austin:** Solomon himself fell prey to high places: "Then Solomon built a high place for Chemosh the detestable idol of Moab … and for Molech the detestable idol of the sons of Ammon" (1 Ki 11:7). This weak point was exploited by his foreign wives who turned his heart after other gods. Josiah's later reforms defiled these same high places (2 Ki 23:13). (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Gill:** This aggravates Israel's sin — they converted and applied the good things the Lord gave them to idolatrous uses. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 17 — "You also took the fine jewelry of gold and silver I had given you, and you made male idols with which to prostitute yourself."

- **Enduring Word / Clarke (Methodist):** "*Priapi* are here meant, which were carried about in the ceremonies of Osiris, Bacchus, and Adonis; and were something like the lingam among the Hindoos.… This was done at the worship of Bacchus in Egypt: and they who wish to see more may consult Herodotus lib. ii, c. 48, 49. In this phallic worship the women were principally concerned." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Precept Austin / Dyer:** "Ezekiel used vivid imagery to drive home the truth of the vileness of Jerusalem's sin. He pictured her taking her jewelry to make a phallic image with which she engaged in sex. Similarly the people of Jerusalem took the material benefits given by God to make idols of false gods and committed spiritual adultery with them." (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Precept Austin / Cooper:** "It was wickedly ironic that the people used God's gifts to build shrines and make idols of gods that were nonexistent. They took fine jewelry and constructed male idols and engaged in ritual sex as part of the fertility cult." (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Constable:** The people made phallic images out of God's gifts with which they engaged in sex (cf. Isa 57:8), or perhaps full human figures are in view. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Keil and Delitzsch (via biblehub.com):** The context does not point to idols of any particular kind, but to the many varieties of Baal-worship. There is no solid ground for thinking specifically of Lingam or Phallus worship, of which it is impossible to find the slightest trace among the Israelites. The Moloch worship is specially mentioned in v. 20 as the greatest abomination of the whole. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-20.htm)

---

### v. 18 — "You took your embroidered garments to cover them, and you set My oil and incense before them."

- **Precept Austin:** Israel took the very things given by God for His worship — embroidered cloth, oil, and incense — and offered them to idols. This was flagrant and brazen action against God's holiness and His covenant. If you are married, you can understand how this would feel: it speaks of the longsuffering of God to hold back His hand of wrath in the face of such bold-faced actions. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Keil and Delitzsch (via biblehub.com):** "Setting before them" (the idols) refers to sacrifices offered as food for the gods, as is evident from the technical expression for the sacrificial odour ascending to God (*lereach nichoach*, cf. Lev 1:9, 13). This is not about *lectisternia* (ritual meals set before idols). (biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-20.htm)

---

### v. 19 — "And you set before them as a pleasing aroma the food I had given you — the fine flour, oil, and honey that I had fed you."

- **Precept Austin:** The very food God provided — fine flour, oil, and honey — was offered to idols as a "soothing aroma" (using the same technical sacrificial language applied to offerings to Yahweh). This is the height of ingratitude and sacrilege. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

- **Gill:** The good things the Lord gave them — both in the wilderness and especially in the land of Canaan — they applied to idolatrous uses. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html)

---

### v. 20 — "You even took the sons and daughters you bore to Me and sacrificed them as food to idols. Was your prostitution not enough?"

- **Pulpit Commentary (via biblehub.com):** "The next stage of idolatry is that of Moloch worship, which never wholly ceased as long as the monarchy of Judah lasted (2 Ki 16:3; Ps 106:37; Isa 57:5; Jer 7:32; 19:5; Mic 6:7; Lev 18:21; 20:2)." (biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-20.htm)

- **Ellicott:** "Hast sacrificed unto them, i.e., hast sacrificed the children unto the idols. This was a terrible development of the later idolatries of Israel. At first the custom appears to have been a ceremony of passing young children through the fire to thereby consecrate them to Moloch; but afterwards it became an actual sacrifice of them in the fire to the idol." Ellicott notes the significant shift in pronouns: in v. 20 they are "thy children whom thou hast borne unto Me" (given by God to Israel), but in v. 21 God calls them "My children" — the sin being aggravated by giving to the idol that which belonged to Jehovah. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-16.html)

- **Enduring Word / Block:** "Instead of presenting her children to Yahweh, her husband, this woman presented them as food to the pagan images that she had made! The expression *le ekol* (lit. 'for eating') portrays the children as idols' diet." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Precept Austin:** Were your harlotries so small a matter? The NLT renders it: "Was it not enough that you should be a prostitute?" — as though idolatry alone were not sufficient, they added infanticide to it. (preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

---

### v. 21 — "You slaughtered My children and delivered them up through the fire to idols."

- **Enduring Word:** "By causing them to pass through the fire" — the pagan god (or demon) Molech was worshipped by heating a metal statue until it was red hot, then placing a living infant on its outstretched hands while beating drums drowned out the screams. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word:** Historical examples: Solomon at least sanctioned Molech worship and built a temple to this idol (1 Ki 11:7). The northern tribes' worship of Molech led to the Assyrian captivity (2 Ki 17:17). King Manasseh of Judah gave his son to Molech (2 Ki 21:6). Up to the days of King Josiah, Molech worship continued because he destroyed a place of worship to that idol (2 Ki 23:10). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Enduring Word (archaeological note):** There is little or no archaeological evidence for child sacrifice among the Israelites of this period. This means that either the practice was very rare or diligently covered up. This may be God's way of saying that even if the practice was rare, it was an abomination to Him. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

- **Keil and Delitzsch (via biblehub.com):** The revulsion of feeling is shown in the reproachful question. The Hebrew *ha-me'at* (was it too little?) is comparative: "was thy whoredom, already described in vv. 16–19, too little, that thou didst also slaughter thy children to idols?" The indignation comes out still more strongly: "thou didst slay *my* sons" (whereas v. 20 said "thy sons, whom thou hast born to me"). *He'evir* (pass through) is used not merely for lustration or februation by fire, but for the actual burning of the children slain as sacrifices. Ezekiel has the Molech-worship in view in the form it had assumed from the times of Ahaz downwards. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-20.htm)

- **Constable:** Jerusalem went so far as slaying her own children as sacrifices to idols, disregarding that they were also the Lord's children (2 Ki 16:3; 21:6; 23:10; 2 Chr 28:3; Jer 32:35; cf. Lev 18:21; 20:1–5; Deut 12:30–32). Evidently the idolaters first slew the children and then burned their dead bodies as sacrifices. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/ezekiel-16.html)

## Traditions Compared — Key Distinctives

### Reformed / Covenant Theology (Ligonier, Calvin)

The Reformed reading emphasises the covenant structure of the chapter. Ligonier frames it as God first acting as adoptive Father (vv. 1–7), then as loving Husband (vv. 8–14) — the two metaphors showing God's sovereign grace. Israel contributed nothing; she was helpless and pagan. The marriage covenant at Sinai is central. The Reformed stress that God's covenant faithfulness contrasts with Israel's unfaithfulness, and the promise of an "everlasting covenant" (vv. 60–63) points to the New Covenant fulfilled in Christ. (learn.ligonier.org/devotionals/faithless-bride-god; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cal/ezekiel-16.html)

### Baptist (Gill, Spurgeon, Garner-Howes)

Baptist commentators like Gill apply the allegory directly to the doctrine of election and effectual calling: the foundling represents God's elect — helpless, polluted, deserving wrath — whom God sovereignly passes by and quickens. The marriage covenant prefigures the covenant of grace made from everlasting and manifested at conversion. Spurgeon draws application for believers: when we begin to worship God's gifts (wealth, health, children, learning) rather than God Himself, we breach the marriage covenant between our soul and God. Garner-Howes emphasises the Baptist distinctives of the New Covenant being "not by national covenant at Sinai but solely by His grace" (citing Gal 3:13–14; 4:26) and sees the everlasting covenant as fulfilled in the Golden Millennial era and the New Covenant of Jeremiah 31. (studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-16.html; enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/; studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ghb/ezekiel-16.html)

### Pentecostal / Charismatic (Enduring Word — David Guzik)

The Enduring Word commentary (widely used in charismatic and Pentecostal circles) stresses the emotional passion of God: the repeated "Live!" shows God's deep feeling. The application is strongly devotional — F. B. Meyer is quoted calling believers to "dare to believe" that in Christ they are more than tolerated, they are loved and arrayed in fair garments. The "trust in your own beauty" warning is applied directly to the believer: the gifts of the Spirit, spiritual success, or fame can become idols. The commentary also emphasises the supernatural dimension: Molech worship was demonic. (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

### Methodist / Holiness (Clarke, Wiersbe — via Enduring Word & Precept Austin)

Adam Clarke (Methodist) focused on the historical-cultural practices behind the text — describing the exposure of infants by heathen nations and the phallic worship associated with Bacchus and Osiris. Wiersbe (though broadly evangelical) brings the Holiness emphasis: Israel "didn't simply occasionally commit adultery, as wicked as that is. She became a professional prostitute" — sin escalates. The root is pride and ingratitude. The warning is that idolatry was Israel's besetting sin and "wasn't cured until the nation was exiled for seventy years in Babylon." (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/; preceptaustin.org/ezekiel_1615-34)

### Lutheran

I was unable to retrieve specific Lutheran commentary from LCMS or 1517.org within the search limits. The general Lutheran approach would emphasise Law and Gospel: the chapter's brutal exposure of sin (Law) drives the hearer to despair of self-righteousness, while the promise of an everlasting covenant in vv. 60–63 (Gospel) points to God's unilateral grace in Christ.

## Other Views

### Modern Scholarship (Block, via Enduring Word)

Daniel Block's NICOT commentary (cited extensively at Enduring Word) provides the most detailed scholarly background. Key insights: (1) The neglect of the newborn — cutting the cord, washing, salting, swaddling — were "customary legal acts of legitimation"; their omission meant the parent legally relinquished all rights. (2) The declaration "Live!" reflects ancient Near Eastern adoption ritual. (3) The shift from nakedness-as-vulnerability to nakedness-as-moral-exposure at puberty. (4) The word *znh* (harlot) occurs 21 times in the chapter — the innocent young woman "graciously elevated to the status of queen, has become a whore." (5) The children sacrificed are portrayed as "idols' diet" (*le ekol*, "for eating"). (enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-16/)

### Keil and Delitzsch (via biblehub.com)

This older, linguistically rigorous commentary cautions against reading phallic worship into v. 17: "it is impossible to find the slightest trace among the Israelites." The "male images" refer broadly to the varieties of Baal-worship. The expression "set before them" refers to sacrifices as food for the gods, using the technical sacrificial language of Leviticus. *He'evir* (pass through the fire) means actual burning of children slain as sacrifices, not merely ritual lustration. (biblehub.com/commentaries/ezekiel/16-20.htm)

### Catholic and Orthodox

I was unable to retrieve specific Catholic or Orthodox commentary within the search limits. The Catholic tradition (e.g., patristic readings) often reads this chapter typologically — Jerusalem as a type of the Church, and the marital imagery as foreshadowing Christ and His Bride. The Orthodox tradition, especially in liturgical use, would read the chapter during Lenten periods as a call to repentance, emphasising God's mercy toward the penitent (as in the closing verses 60–63).

## Summary of Key Points Across Traditions

| Theme | Shared Emphasis |
|---|---|
| **Grace alone** | All traditions agree: Israel's beauty and status came entirely from God's unmerited grace — she was a despised, abandoned foundling with no claim on Him. |
| **Covenant marriage** | The spreading of the skirt and the covenant at Sinai is universally seen as a marriage covenant between Yahweh and Israel. |
| **Pride as the root sin** | "You trusted in your own beauty" (v. 15) is identified across traditions as the turning point — pride in gifts received rather than in the Giver. |
| **Idolatry as spiritual adultery** | All traditions read the harlotry imagery as depicting idolatry — running after pagan gods and political alliances. |
| **Child sacrifice as the ultimate horror** | Molech worship is universally seen as the nadir of Israel's apostasy — sacrificing God's own children to idols. |
| **Hope beyond judgment** | Though beyond vv. 1–21, all traditions note the chapter ends with the promise of an everlasting covenant (vv. 60–63) — pointing to restoration and ultimately to Christ. |
